1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5.name: Ruy Lopez
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5.background: Named after Ruy López de Segura, a Spanish priest who analysed it in his book of 1561, although the Göttingen manuscript of about 1490 already contains it. It became widely popular only in the mid-nineteenth century, after Carl Jaenisch published a detailed article on 1.e4 e5 in 1847.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6.strategy: The question to the bishop that defines the main line: Black finds out at once whether White means to give up the bishop for the knight. If White takes, Black gets the two bishops for doubled pawns; if White retreats, the bishop stays aimed at the knight that guards e5 but can be chased again with ...b5 whenever Black likes.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a threat to e4 and simply ignores the bishop: Black can take the pawn and White regains it, so nothing is lost. The line leads to solid, drawish positions, often an early queen trade in which Black has the bishop pair against a kingside pawn majority.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nge7.name: Ruy Lopez: Cozio Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nge7.background: Carl Jaenisch dismissed it in his mid-nineteenth-century analysis of the Ruy Lopez, and Bent Larsen later used it occasionally with success.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nge7.strategy: Defends the knight with the other knight, so after a capture on c6 Black recaptures with the knight and keeps the pawns intact. The cost is that the knight blocks the king's bishop. An old-fashioned, little-explored set-up that avoids the main-line theory.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and sets up on the long diagonal instead of defending e5 with a pawn. Quiet and solid but slow, so White can open the centre quickly and aim for a small edge; rarely played today.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Be7.name: Ruy Lopez: Lucena Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Be7.strategy: A flexible developing move that prepares castling and expects to reach the main line of the Ruy Lopez by transposition. But Black has not yet put the question to the bishop, so White keeps more options open.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nd4.name: Ruy Lopez: Bird Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nd4.background: Published in 1843 in Paul Rudolf von Bilguer's Handbuch des Schachspiels and explored by Henry Bird in the late nineteenth century; Bird played it as Black at least 25 times, scoring nine wins, thirteen losses and three draws. No strong master since Bird has adopted it regularly.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nd4.strategy: Counterattacks the bishop and the knight on f3 at once, a surprise that offers a trade. If White takes, Black recaptures with the pawn and gains space, but at the price of a slightly worse pawn structure. With careful play White is held to keep a small edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6.name: Ruy Lopez: Steinitz Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6.background: The favourite of the first world champion, Wilhelm Steinitz, and often played by Emanuel Lasker and José Raúl Capablanca. It largely fell into disuse after the First World War.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6.strategy: Defends e5 directly with a pawn, solid but passive and cramped. The pawn takes the king's bishop's best diagonal, and White can strike in the centre at once and force Black to give up the e5 pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5.strategy: Strikes at the e4 pawn from the flank and sacrifices material for a kingside attack, ignoring the bishop. Sharp and a good practical weapon, but positionally risky: it loosens Black's own kingside and against a prepared opponent Black can end up in trouble.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5.name: Ruy Lopez: Classical Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5.background: Possibly the oldest defence to the Ruy Lopez, played occasionally by Boris Spassky and Boris Gulko.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop on the active diagonal toward f2 without worrying about the pressure on c6. But White can drive it back with pawn moves that also build the centre, so Black loses time; rarely played.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bb4.name: Ruy Lopez: Alapin Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bb4.strategy: Puts the bishop on an active diagonal but does nothing about the pressure on c6 and e5. White kicks it at once with a pawn move that also builds the centre, so Black loses time for little in return.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a5.name: Ruy Lopez: Bulgarian Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a5.strategy: A queenside pawn move that does nothing about the pressure on c6 and e5. Its only point is a trap: if White drifts, the bishop can be shut in on the queenside. Against sensible play Black has simply lost time.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f6.name: Ruy Lopez: Nürnberg Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn but takes the natural f6 square from the king's knight and weakens the kingside, so Black's development becomes awkward and White is left with the easier game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 b6.name: Ruy Lopez: Rotary-Albany Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 b6.strategy: Prepares to put the bishop on the long diagonal but ignores the pressure on c6 and e5, and loosens the queenside. The gambit idea is dubious and White gets a comfortable game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Qe7.name: Ruy Lopez: Vinogradov Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Qe7.strategy: Protects e5 at once, but the queen blocks the king's bishop and is tied to a passive defence. Not refuted, yet Black's development is awkward and White develops with ease.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g5.name: Ruy Lopez: Brentano Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g5.strategy: A reckless pawn thrust that aims to chase the knight from f3 but develops nothing and does nothing for e5. It cripples the kingside, so White can strike in the centre while Black's king is exposed.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Na5.name: Ruy Lopez: Pollock Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Na5.strategy: Sidesteps the bishop but takes the only defender away from e5, so White can capture the pawn at once. The knight on the rim does little, and Black has spent a move on a bad square.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nb8.name: Ruy Lopez: Retreat Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nb8.strategy: Retreats the knight to where it started: Black wastes two moves, gives up the defence of e5, which White can capture at once, and has asked nothing of the bishop. A curiosity rather than a defence.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d5.name: Ruy Lopez: Spanish Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d5.strategy: Counterattacks in the centre at once, offering White the choice between two central pawns. But Black is behind in development and the bishop still presses on c6: if White takes on d5 and the queen recaptures, Nc3 hits it with gain of time.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bb4 4.c3.strategy: Hits the bishop at once and prepares d4. The black bishop, which only copies White's move and attacks nothing undefended, must retreat or be exchanged, so White builds a broad pawn centre with tempo.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bb4 4.Bxc6.strategy: Doubles Black's pawns at once, trusting the structure to tell in the long run. Black gets the bishop pair, and after the usual ...dxc6 the grab on e5 is not free, since ...Qd4 regains the pawn: a small, safe edge but no initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bb4 4.O-O.strategy: Castles and ignores the wandering bishop, which attacks nothing that is not defended. Sound and flexible, but it neither doubles Black's pawns nor gains the tempo that c3 does, so White's edge is smaller.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bb4 4.c3 Ba5.strategy: Keeps the bishop on the diagonal towards White's king instead of retreating to c5, but it leaves e5 hanging to Bxc6 and Nxe5, and the c3 pawn takes away the d4 square that would let Black's queen win the pawn back. Black ends up a pawn down for the bishop pair.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bb4 4.c3 Bc5.strategy: Retreats to the active diagonal towards f2, keeping an eye on White's king. The price is time: White has c3 for free, so d4 builds a broad centre with a tempo, and Black has to play against it with pieces.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bb4 4.c3 Be7.strategy: Retreats all the way home. The bishop is safe from every attack, but it is passive on e7 and Black has lost a tempo, so White builds the centre without hindrance and Black spends the game catching up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bb4 4.c3 Ba5 5.B.strategy: Takes the knight before Black can regroup: after either recapture the e5 pawn is loose, and ...Qd4 is no longer a defence because the c3 pawn covers d4. White wins a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bb4 4.c3 Ba5 5.O.strategy: Castles first. Nothing hangs, but the chance to exploit the loose e5 pawn passes: Black gets a move to defend it or to counterattack e4, and the grip of the c3 pawn on d4 matters less. Sound but slow.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bb4 4.c3 Ba5 5.B.strategy: Retreats and keeps the bishop, avoiding the exchange. It also gives up the quick pawn win: Black gets time to defend e5, so the game settles into a calmer fight in which White has no obvious edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bb4 4.c3 Ba5 5.B.name: Ruy Lopez: Alapin Defence, Alapin Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bb4 4.c3 Ba5 5.B.strategy: The natural recapture: it opens the d-file and the c8 bishop and keeps the bishop pair. The e5 pawn cannot be held, since c3 takes d4 away from the queen, so Black plays for quick development and the bishops in return for it.

Recaptures with the b-pawn to keep the d-pawn at home and open the b-file, but the queenside pawns become ragged and the a-pawn isolated. The e5 pawn falls just the same, so Black is a pawn down with little to show for it.
Takes the c3 pawn, but White recaptures and Black's bishop is gone for a pawn: after the exchange on c6 Black is left a piece down for a pawn with nothing in return.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.c3.name: Ruy Lopez: Classical Variation, Central Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.c3.strategy: Prepares d4, which would hit the bishop with tempo, and covers d4, so Black can no longer count on ...Qd4 to defend e5. Bxc6 and Nxe5 become a real threat, which makes this the most critical answer to the early bishop.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.O-O.strategy: Castles first and prepares to defend e4 with the rook, but the king goes onto the diagonal of Black's bishop, so the f2 pawn is pinned and the rook may be tied to f1. Calm, positional play with a small edge for White rather than a sharp central fight.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.b4.name: Ruy Lopez: Classical Variation, Spanish Wing Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.b4.strategy: Sacrifices the b-pawn to pull Black's bishop off its diagonal and then gain time with c3 and a pawn centre. Black can take the pawn and retreat with the extra material, and White must prove that the centre and open lines pay for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.c3 Bb6.name: Ruy Lopez: Classical Variation, Charousek Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.c3 Bb6.strategy: Steps back before d4 can hit it, keeping the bishop on the diagonal towards f2 and out of reach of the pawns. White gets to build its broad centre, so Black has to undermine it with piece play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.c3 Qe7.name: Ruy Lopez: Classical Defence, Boden Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.c3 Qe7.strategy: Defends e5 a second time and prepares to meet d4 with a retreat of the bishop to b6. Playable, but it brings the queen out early, blocks the e7 square, and leaves White free to build the full pawn centre it came for.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.c3 f5.name: Ruy Lopez: Classical Variation, Cordel Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.c3 f5.strategy: Counterattacks e4 at once, a sharp pawn offer that weakens the king. The better way to meet it is to strike in the centre with d4, while the weakened e8-h5 diagonal soon invites a queen check.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.c3 d5.name: Ruy Lopez: Classical Variation, Konikowski Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.c3 d5.strategy: Strikes at e4 with the d-pawn, but that opens the diagonal e8-b5 and leaves the c6 knight pinned against the king. White can take on d5 or win time with Nxe5 against the pinned knight, so Black's centre play comes at the cost of tied-up pieces and a risky king.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a counterattack on e4, so an exchange on c6 followed by Nxe5 only trades pawns, since ...Nxe4 wins the pawn back. Black meets the big centre White wants with quick development and a sound, flexible game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.O-O Nd4.strategy: Hits the Spanish bishop and challenges the knight on f3 that attacks e5. If White trades, Black can recapture with the bishop and keep a sound pawn structure, but White then gains time with c3 and builds a pawn centre while the bishop retreats. A positional line with slight pressure for White.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6.strategy: Develops with a counterattack on e4, so an exchange on c6 and the capture on e5 only trades pawns. Black keeps the bishop active and aims for a solid game in which White has only a small initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.O-O Nge7.strategy: Develops the second knight and adds a defender to c6, so an exchange there can be answered by a knight and no pawns are doubled. The knight on e7 is passive and does not touch e4, so White keeps the freer centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.O-O Nd4 5..name: Ruy Lopez: Classical Defence, Zaitsev Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5 4.O-O Nd4 5..strategy: A gambit that offers the b-pawn to pull the bishop away from c5, the square from which it guards the knight on d4. Black can simply take the pawn, so White has to prove the activity is worth it; the quiet exchange on d4 asks far less of White.

Removes the knight that attacks the Spanish bishop and the f3 knight, so Black has to recapture. After the bishop recaptures, White gains time with a central pawn; after the pawn recaptures, the structure is fixed. Either way White keeps a small, safe edge and a clear plan.
Retreats and leaves the d4 knight alone, so Black can trade it on f3. White keeps both bishops after the queen recaptures, but it has spent time on the retreat and Black's centre stays intact.
Retreats to the diagonal aimed at f7. If Black trades on f3, the queen recaptures with a double attack on f7, so Black has to spend a move defending it. White keeps both bishops and some initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d5 4.Nxe5.strategy: Wins a pawn that the pinned c6 knight cannot take back. Grabbing e4 in return loses to Nxc6 bxc6 Bxc6+, which wins the rook on a8, so Black needs a sharper answer, while White must watch for forks against the loose knight and the g2 pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d5 4.exd5.strategy: Takes the d-pawn and keeps the c6 knight pinned, so Black must recapture with the queen. Nc3 then hits it at once, and the pinned knight cannot help the loose e5 pawn, so White gains time and keeps the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d5 4.c3.strategy: Builds the centre with d4 in mind instead of taking either pawn. It gives up the clean gain that taking on d5 or e5 offers: after ...dxe4 White can only win the pawn back with Nxe5, so the extra pawn is gone.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d5 4.Nxe5 Qg5.strategy: Forks the unprotected knight on e5 and the g2 pawn, which nothing defends while White's king is still on e1. White has to find the careful reply, since the natural-looking ones lose material; it is Black's trickiest try in this counter-gambit.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d5 4.Nxe5 Bd7.strategy: Breaks the pin so that the knight can take on e5, setting a trap: after exd5? Nxe5 and the bishop trade on d7, Black is a piece up for two pawns. White simply trades on d7 first and then takes on d5, staying a pawn up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d5 4.Nxe5 dxe4.strategy: Takes the e-pawn back at once but walks into Nxc6 bxc6 Bxc6+: the check wins the rook on a8, so Black loses an exchange or more with nothing in return.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d5 4.Nxe5 Qg5 5..name: Ruy Lopez: Spanish Countergambit, Harding Countergambit, Fricke Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d5 4.Nxe5 Qg5 5..strategy: Castles to cover g2 and lets Black take the knight, hoping to win two pawns back with exd5 while the c6 knight is pinned and Black's king sits in the centre. A knight for two pawns is too much to give, and simply retreating the knight keeps White better.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d5 4.Nxe5 Qg5 5..name: Ruy Lopez: Spanish Countergambit, Harding Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d5 4.Nxe5 Qg5 5..strategy: Takes the knight but walks into the point of the queen move: with the king still on e1 nothing guards g2, so ...Qxg2 attacks the rook on h1 and the queen then takes e4 with check. White ends a pawn down with a king stuck in the centre.

The careful retreat: the knight attacks the queen at once and covers g1, so a grab on g2 meets Rg1 with tempo. White keeps the extra pawn from e5, and Black's pinned knight and king in the centre stay as targets.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4.name: Ruy Lopez: Steinitz Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4.background: Wilhelm Steinitz did not fully appreciate 4.d4, which is today understood to be the most critical continuation.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4.strategy: Attacks e5 a second time and, with the c6 knight pinned, genuinely threatens to win the pawn. Black must trade pawns or break the pin, so White forces the issue at once and gets a lasting space advantage whichever way Black decides.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.O-O.strategy: Castles first and keeps the central break in hand. The pressure on e5 is relaxed for a move, so Black can organise its cramped defence, but White has lost nothing and can strike in the centre whenever it likes.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.c3.strategy: Prepares a broad pawn centre and a quiet d4. It takes the natural square from the b1 knight and is slower than striking at once, which gives Black time to hit back at the centre with the f-pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops and guards e4, keeping d4 in reserve. It blocks the c-pawn, so the pawn centre has to be built with d4 alone, and it hands Black a free move to arrange its defence.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7.strategy: Breaks the pin and defends the pawn on e5 in one move: an exchange on c6 can now be answered by the bishop, so nothing is won on e5. Black keeps the stronghold, at the price of a cramped position in which the d6 pawn shuts in the dark-squared bishop.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Trades pawns before White can win one, but gives up the stronghold on e5. White's knight recaptures into the centre and keeps a lasting space edge, so Black must defend a cramped but solid position.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Nf6.strategy: Counterattacks e4, but the pin on c6 makes it fail: dxe5 Nxe4 allows Qd5, which attacks the knight and f7 together, and Black loses at least a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.strategy: Guards e4 and renews the threat to e5: after the exchange on c6 and the capture on e5 the e4 pawn can no longer be won back by the bishop, so a pawn is really at stake. White develops and keeps the initiative while Black stays cramped.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.c4.name: Ruy Lopez: Steinitz Defence, Semi-Duras Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.c4.strategy: Gains space on the queenside but, instead of guarding e4, leaves it undefended, so the threat against e5 is gone: Black can trade on d4 or attack e4 with a developing move. White settles for a space edge with a looser centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.d5.strategy: Gains space and kicks the c6 knight at once, giving up the pressure on e5 for a closed centre. Once the bishops are traded, White keeps a lasting space advantage in a slow manoeuvring game against a cramped Black position.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4, so that capturing on e5 no longer wins a pawn: ...Bxe4 or ...Nxe4 regains it at once. Black completes development and holds the centre solidly.
Gives up the e5 stronghold, but removes the target at once, so no pawn can be won there. White's knight recaptures in the centre with more space, and Black gets a solid but cramped position.
Develops and prepares to castle, but leaves e4 unattacked, so White wins the e5 pawn: Bxc6 Bxc6 dxe5 dxe5 Qxd8+ Bxd8 Nxe5, and the bishop cannot take e4 because the knight on c3 guards it.

Brings the king to safety and keeps all the pressure on e5 and the option of exchanging on c6. It is the sound way to continue development; Black must soon decide how to resolve the tension in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.name: Ruy Lopez: Steinitz Defence, Nimzowitsch Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.strategy: Trades the bishop for the knight to remove a defender of e5, but Black recaptures with the bishop, so the pawn structure stays intact and e5 is not really attacked. White gives up the bishop pair for little in return.

Pins the f6 knight against the queen, the piece that makes capturing on e5 unprofitable, and threatens to remove it. Black breaks the pin and the exchanges that follow leave e5 safe, so White gains little.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.name: Ruy Lopez: Berlin Defence, Hedgehog Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.strategy: Develops the bishop and prepares to castle, but only once the centre is settled: with White's rook heading for e1, castling at once runs into a tactic that loses material, so Black will have to exchange on d4. Solid, but passive.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.name: Ruy Lopez: Berlin Defence, Closed Wolf Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.strategy: Resolves the centre at once, before White's rook reaches the e-file, and so avoids the tactics around castling. The price is the e5 stronghold: White's knight recaptures into the centre with a freer game, but Black's pieces are well placed and the structure is sound.

Defends e5 once more, but the queen takes the natural square of the f8 bishop, so Black is slow to castle. Sound enough, yet it leaves Black cramped and White free to choose when to resolve the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 exd4 5.O.name: Ruy Lopez: Steinitz Defence, Centre Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 exd4 5.O.strategy: Castles before recapturing on d4. The pinned c6 knight cannot take the pawn, and unpinning with ...Bd7 just lets White recapture. A harmless delay that gains nothing over the direct recapture and lets Black try to keep the pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 exd4 5.N.strategy: Recaptures in the centre with a developing move: the pinned knight on c6 cannot take it, so White keeps a lasting space advantage and Black must find a way to unpin and develop. A small but safe edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 exd4 5.Q.strategy: Recaptures with the queen, which the pinned knight cannot challenge for the moment. The queen is exposed once Black unpins, so White loses time, and Black gets a comfortable game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 exd4 5.B.strategy: Trades the bishop for the knight before recapturing on d4: Black's queenside pawns are damaged, but White gives up the bishop pair and the pin, and Black gets two bishops in an open position. Playable, with a small structural plus.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nd4 4.Nxd4.strategy: Takes the knight at once: White gives Black no time to profit from the attack on the bishop. Black recaptures with the pawn and gains space on d4 at the cost of doubled pawns and a lag in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nd4 4.Bc4.strategy: Withdraws the bishop to the diagonal aimed at f7 instead of capturing. Black usually trades the knights and White recaptures with the queen, which keeps White developing quickly and the position flexible.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nd4 4.Be2.strategy: Retreats to a safe but passive square. Black can trade knights and White recaptures with the bishop, which is sound but leaves White with a modest game and no initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nd4 4.Nxd4 exd4.strategy: The only sensible recapture. The pawn on d4 cramps White's queenside development and is not easy to dislodge, but Black has doubled pawns and is behind in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nd4 4.Nxd4 c6.strategy: Attacks the bishop while the e5 pawn also hits the knight on d4, but White takes on c6 first: after ...dxc6 the bishop retreats. Black wins the piece back only at the cost of a clean pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5.strategy: Attacks the knight on d4 instead of retaking it, but White simply retreats the knight and keeps the extra piece.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nd4 4.Nxd4 exd4.strategy: Castles at once: the pawn on d4 cannot be attacked quickly, so White builds a solid position, closes the centre and waits for the doubled pawns and the lag in development to tell.

Puts the bishop on a more active diagonal aimed at f7, where ...c6 no longer gains a tempo. It sets a trap: if Black develops the knight and takes on e4, Bxf7+ and Qh5+ win the pawn back with the king dragged into the open. Often leads to more piece trades.

Guards the e4 pawn and opens the c1-bishop, aiming for the same solid set-up as the main move by a different route. It does not hurry: Black's ...c6 can still chase the bishop, and the pawn on d4 keeps cramping White's centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nd4 4.Nxd4 exd4.name: Ruy Lopez: Bird Variation, Paulsen Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nd4 4.Nxd4 exd4.strategy: Quiet development: the knight heads for g6 or f5 and ...c6 can follow to chase the bishop, but it shuts the f8 bishop's diagonal for now. Black keeps the space-gaining pawn on d4 but is behind in development, which White will try to exploit.

The most common reply: the bishop guards the advanced d4 pawn and clears e7 for the knight, since ...Nf6 would be driven back by e5. Black is behind in development, so getting the kingside pieces out and castling comes first, while the extra space on d4 stays.

Kicks the bishop at once and prepares ...d5 to widen the centre, gaining time while White's bishop looks for a square. The cost is development: Black's kingside pieces stay at home, so the centre must not open against a king that has not castled.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nge7 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight rather than castling and keeps a central strike in reserve. With Black's bishop still shut in behind the knight on e7, White can choose the moment to open the centre, and d5 is a good square to aim at.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nge7 4.O-O.strategy: Castles before committing the centre and keeps the bishop's pressure on the knight that guards e5. Black must now decide how to free the king's bishop, by a fianchetto or by bringing the knight back, while White builds up without risk. The main answer to this set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nge7 4.c3.strategy: Prepares d4 to take a broad pawn centre while Black's king's bishop is still shut in behind the knight on e7. It is a plan for space rather than speed, and it leaves the king in the centre a little longer than castling would.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nge7 4.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once. It is sound, but the exchanges that follow ease the cramp in Black's set-up, so White gains little more than a comfortable game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nge7 4.Nc3 g6.name: Ruy Lopez: Cozio Defence, Paulsen Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nge7 4.Nc3 g6.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop to the long diagonal, solving the problem of the bishop shut in behind the knight on e7. But Black's pieces are slow to coordinate: White can strike in the centre and plant a knight on d5 with the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nge7 4.Nc3 Ng6.strategy: Brings the knight to the square where it guards e5 and frees the king's bishop at once. If White takes on c6, Black recaptures with the d-pawn and has the bishop pair for the doubled pawns; otherwise Black has a compact set-up that sidesteps the fight for d5 the fianchetto invites.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nge7 4.Nc3 a6.strategy: Puts the question to the bishop at once. If White exchanges on c6, Black recaptures with the knight and keeps a sound pawn structure; if the bishop retreats, Black gains queenside space. But the knight on e7 still blocks the king's bishop, and a pawn move has not helped development.
